metadata.display_heading: Mixed-Model Estimation of Direct and Associative Effects

blocks.content: The general approach follows if we consider a standard animal model with additional random effects (Equations 19.20 and 19.21). Equation 22.1b shows how the phenotype of individual i is the sum of its direct breeding value, the social breeding values of its group members, and the environmental effects, [[SEE_FORMULA:22.38a]]

To start, we assume a very simple residual structure [[SEE_FORMULA:22.38b]] where the $ e_i $ are uncorrelated and homoscedastic, so that $ \mathbf{e} \sim (\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{e}))\mathbf{I} $. Letting $ \mathbf{a}_d $ denote the vector of direct breeding values (DBVs), and $ \mathbf{a}_s $ be the vector of social breeding values (SBVs), the resulting mixed model becomes [[SEE_FORMULA:22.38c]]

Here $ \beta $ is the vector of fixed effects (which will be just the mean for our simple example) and X is the design matrix associated with these fixed effects. Likewise, $ Z_{d} $ and $ Z_{s} $ are the corresponding incidence matrices for the direct and social effects, which follow logically upon considering the group members (Examples 22.10 and 22.11).

To complete the model, we need to specify the covariance structures of the three vectors of random effects. Our initial assumption on the residual errors implies that the covariance matrix for the residuals is $ \sigma^2(e) $. The covariance structure for the two vectors of random effects is a function of the relationship matrix A (Chapter 19) of the individuals in the study, which has block-matrix form. [[SEE_FORMULA:22.39a]]

This is often written more compactly using the Kronecker or direct product notation as $ \mathbf{G} \otimes \mathbf{A} $, where [[SEE_FORMULA:22.39b]] Because the residuals are assumed to be uncorrelated with the other random effects, the full covariance structure for this model is [[SEE_FORMULA:22.39c]]
